name: Bronzing drops

lead: Bronzing or self-tan drops are concentrated tanning formulas, usually based on dihydroxyacetone (DHA), that are added to a moisturiser or serum so the user controls how deep the colour gets.

The appeal is a tan-like complexion on the face or body without sun or tanning beds. DHA reacts with amino acids in the outer skin layer to darken it, and the colour fades over several days as skin sheds.

paras: Users blend a few drops into a facial or body moisturiser, apply it, and build colour over repeated uses; more drops give a deeper shade. Brand instructions typically ask for even blending to avoid streaks.

Colour can look streaky or orange if blended poorly. The FDA has approved DHA for external use only and not around the eyes, on lips or by inhalation. DHA products can cause contact dermatitis in some people, and dermatologists generally advise sunscreen alongside self-tanner.

angle.text: The drops add a bronze tone to the face or body without sun, and the user adjusts depth by mixing more or fewer drops. The colour is temporary and fades as skin cells shed.

lead: Bronzing drops are concentrated self-tanning products designed to be mixed into the user's own moisturiser. Most use dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a three-carbon sugar that, according to cosmetic chemist Nicole Pozniak, reacts with amino acids in the stratum corneum to produce a tanned appearance [1].

They help someone look tanned without UV exposure and let the user tune the intensity by the number of drops. A New Beauty guide describes L'Oreal Paris Sublime Bronze Self-Tanning Drops as a face option used by mixing several drops with moisturiser, and notes that drops have become popular for a natural-looking facial glow [1].
Houston dermatologist Jennifer Segal told New Beauty she favours self-tanners because they give a tanned look without UV-associated skin cancer risk, while still recommending SPF [1].
infobox: FDA: DHA approved for external use only
DHA's tanning effect found in the 1950s (Eva Wittgenstein)

paras: Drops are one form of sunless tanner alongside lotions, mousses, sprays and booths. DHA is typically used at about 3-5 percent in sunless tanners, with higher concentrations giving darker shades; some formulas add erythrulose, which develops more slowly [2][1].

DHA's skin-darkening effect was discovered by Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital in the 1950s; Man-Tan launched in 1959 and Coppertone's QT in 1960, and early orange results hurt the category's image. Gradual-tan lotions and, from the late 1990s, spray booths broadened the market [2].
DHA does not dye the skin; it reacts with amino acids in dead outer skin cells, producing browning without UV. The colour fades over roughly 3-10 days as skin sheds [2][1].

The FDA has approved DHA for external use only, and not around the eyes, on lips or mucous membranes, or by inhalation [2]. DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis, and fragrances and other ingredients in formulas are listed as common allergens [2]. A 2007 study found increased free-radical formation in DHA-treated skin under sun exposure, and sun protection is advised for at least a day after application [2]. Self-tanner does not itself protect against UV [1].
No studies found on tanning drops specifically. Research on DHA self-tanners in general is summarised in Wikipedia's overview of sunless tanning [2].

timeline.event: Eva Wittgenstein discovers DHA's tanning effect [2].
